questions.q: What does `@Cacheable` do on a method?
o: Returns the cached result for the same key and skips the method
Runs the method twice in a row for extra safety
Stores the result as a new row in a database table
Caches only the exceptions that the method throws
questions.w: It is implemented by a proxy (cache-aside). On a miss it runs the method and stores the result under the key.

questions.q: Which annotation removes stale data after an update?
o: `@CacheEvict`
`@Cacheable`
`@CacheConfig`
`@EnableCaching`
questions.w: `@CachePut` updates the entry with the new value and always runs the method. `@CacheEvict` removes entries.

o: A hot entry expires and many requests hit the source at once
The cache runs out of disk space under heavy load
Two caches end up holding different copies of data
A cache key collides with another key of the same hash
questions.w: Mitigate with `sync = true`, jittered TTLs, request coalescing or refresh-ahead.

questions.q: Why should cached account balances usually have a short TTL, or not be cached at all?
o: A stale value can mislead users or drive wrong decisions
Caches are not able to store numeric values at all
Balances never change over the life of an account
TTLs are not supported for entries that hold numbers
questions.w: Cache data that is read often, changes rarely and tolerates some staleness. Money values need strict freshness or event-based eviction.

questions.q: A cache lives in each JVM instance (Caffeine). What happens when one instance updates data?
o: Other instances keep stale copies until they expire or are evicted
All the instances update themselves instantly and together
The cache is shared between them automatically by Spring
The update fails with an exception on every other node
questions.w: For shared state use a distributed cache such as Redis, or publish eviction events to all nodes.

questions.q: A `@Async` method is called from another method in the same class. What happens?
o: It runs synchronously, because the call bypasses the proxy
It runs on a new thread, exactly as the annotation suggests
Spring throws an exception when the application starts
It runs twice, once in each of two different threads
questions.w: Like other proxy features, `@Async` works only when called through the bean from outside. Call it from another bean.

questions.q: Why configure a custom `TaskExecutor` for `@Async` instead of relying on defaults?
o: To bound the pool and queue, name threads and handle rejection
Because Spring does not create any default executor at all
To make the methods run in the caller's own thread
To remove the need for a proxy around the bean
questions.w: Unbounded or misconfigured pools can exhaust memory or threads. Name threads for easier debugging.

questions.q: Where does an exception thrown in a `void` `@Async` method go?
o: To the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`; the caller never sees it
Back to the caller, the same as with a normal call
It is retried automatically by Spring a few times
It stops the whole application from running
questions.w: Return a `CompletableFuture` so the caller can handle failures, or register an uncaught exception handler that logs them.
